prize_parts.citation: for the optical lattice clock: magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms and its development to fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I opened with circuit QED (B021) at rank 1, but after reading the other seven ballots I now put the optical lattice clock first. It has the broadest and most robust support: three first places and four top-three rankings. Danielsson, Kroll and Lindroth each place it first on its own scientific merits, and the reasons they give are concrete. The magic-wavelength idea is original and clearly bounded. Many independent national laboratories reproduce clocks at the 10^-18 level, and international comparisons are routine. It opens relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a route to redefining the second. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the clock to record accuracy and stability and linking it to combs) is compact and fits the three-laureate limit with room to spare. The result is a prize about what we can measure and how well, and it is mature rather than early.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier recognition. The 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize on controlling single quantum systems (which touched ion-based optical clocks) both lie close, so the citation must be drawn tightly around neutral-atom lattice trapping and not around optical clocks in general. Credit also lies outside the pair: Lemonde, the Boulder and JILA clock groups and the ion-clock community all contributed. Finally, the redefinition of the second has not yet happened. A prize framed around that outcome would be premature, so the citation has to rest on the demonstrated measurement capability.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a conceptually original, bounded advance in laser spectroscopy, with magic-wavelength trapping removing motional and light-shift errors and enabling parallel interrogation of many atoms; he treats the boundary with the 2005 comb prize and with ion clocks as a matter of framing.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and have moved toward it. I would go further on the framing risk. If the citation reads as optical clocks and frequency standards in general, it collides with 2005 and with the Wineland-related ion-clock work, and Ye's comb-linked programme is the part most exposed. I would keep the citation specific to magic-wavelength lattice trapping and the resulting 10^-18 accuracy and stability. That keeps the prize defined by a single invention that both laureates demonstrably advanced.

responses.point: Pearce ranks IceCube (B054) first as an engineering-plus-physics opening of a new observational window, but concedes that source-level associations are few and statistically modest and that the credit across a large collaboration and earlier DUMAND and Baikal pioneers is hard to reduce to three.
responses.response: I respect the experimental achievement, and the diffuse flux is robust. I still hold back for two reasons. By your own account the source-level astrophysics is still moderate in significance and may shift with KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD data, so the astrophysical story is less settled than the clock result. The attribution problem is also sharper here than for the clock. A two-name lattice-clock prize needs no judgement about who led a collaboration. I would keep B054 as a serious candidate for a later year, not this one.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the cavity method (B025) first and B015 (twisted bilayer graphene) second, arguing that B015's conceptual core is secure even though the superconducting mechanism is debated and recognition may be early.
responses.response: I agree that the magic-angle flat-band prediction and the correlated phases are firmly established. But the unresolved pairing mechanism and the field's age of about eight years make me cautious this year. The credit also leaves out the first author of the discovery experiment and several early confirming groups. For the cavity method, I think the line against the Parisi prize is the real difficulty, and I am not yet persuaded it can be drawn cleanly. Relative to both, the lattice clock has two decades of independent confirmation and a settled interpretation, which is why I put it ahead.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks the lattice clock first and topological insulators (B053) second, noting that the credited list omits Bernevig, Zhang and Hughes, who are arguably essential to the HgTe prediction, and that the third slot is a choice between Mele and Hasan.
responses.response: I share both of your points. The topological-insulator case is scientifically very strong, but any three-name selection from the supplied credit leaves out essential people, and I made an uneasy choice of Hasan over Mele in my own opening ballot. That attribution problem is why I keep B053 as an alternative and not my preference. The lattice clock does not have this difficulty, which is the main reason I now back your first choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can write a citation that separates neutral-atom lattice clocks from the 2005 comb prize and ion-clock work.
Whether the contributions of other lattice-clock groups (for example Lemonde and the Boulder clock community) warrant a different credited set than Katori and Ye alone.
How much weight should be given to the not yet realised redefinition of the second.
If circuit QED (B021) returns later, how much the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits should count as thematic concentration.
statement.conflict_note: I opened with circuit QED (B021) at rank 1. As director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a professor at Chalmers working on circuit and waveguide QED, I have a professional interest in that field, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in it. I should recuse myself or at least discount my judgement on B021 and on closely related superconducting-circuit candidates. No specific personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock community is apparent from my profile.
